pedagogy.summary: At 10-11, the capstone, precision covers the vocabulary of ratio, proportion, algebra, volume, coordinate geometry and circle parts, plus algebraic notation and order of operations. Two distinctions are load-bearing: the parts of a circle (radius is centre-to-circumference, diameter is all the way across = twice the radius, circumference is the distance around), and the difference between an expression, an equation and a formula (an expression has no equals sign; an equation asserts two things are equal; a formula is a general rule relating quantities). Following EEF, pupils should read expressions as descriptions of relationships, not just instructions to calculate, and use precise terms that reflect structure.
bestPractices: Sort algebraic objects into expression / equation / formula by their defining feature — the presence and role of '=' — and read expressions as relationships, not just 'work it out' (EEF; CCSS)
Label a circle so radius, diameter and circumference attach to features, and establish diameter = 2 × radius
Match volume units to the quantity (cm³ fills space) and keep them distinct from area (cm²)
Rephrase informal responses into precise mathematical language, choosing the formal register (EEF; the cross-curricular formal-vocabulary link)
Test definitions with non-examples — 'is 3x + 5 an equation?' — to sharpen the boundaries (EEF)
keyRepresentations: A labelled circle (radius, diameter, circumference) with diameter = 2r shown
Sorting cards: expression (3x+5) vs equation (3x+5=11) vs formula (V=l×w×h)
Ratio/proportion notation (a : b) with a bar or double number line
Order-of-operations worked expressions read as relationships
commonMisconceptions: Conflates expression, equation and formula — calls 3x + 5 an equation, or uses the terms interchangeably
Confuses circle parts — says the diameter is centre-to-edge (that is the radius), or calls the circumference the 'edge'/'side'
Omits the volume unit or uses the wrong dimension — '60' or '60 cm²' instead of '60 cm³'
Reads an algebraic expression only as an instruction to calculate rather than a relationship, mishandling order of operations

learn.summary: For ages 10-11, this capstone strand builds precise mathematical vocabulary and notation: distinguishing an expression (no equals sign; it can be evaluated or simplified but not solved) from an equation (asserts two things are equal; an equation such as 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved) from a formula (a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities); naming circle parts correctly (radius = centre to circumference, diameter = all the way across through the centre = 2 × radius, circumference = the distance around); and attaching the right units to a quantity (volume in cm³, distinct from area in cm²). Following EEF, learners should read expressions as descriptions of relationships, not just instructions to calculate, and use terms that reflect mathematical structure.

activities.title: Sort algebra cards by the role of '='
feedback: If a learner labels '3x + 5' an equation, ask them to point to the equals sign — there is none, so it is an expression you can evaluate (for a given x) or simplify, but not solve.
If a learner cannot separate equation from formula, contrast '3x + 5 = 11' (a claim true for one value of x, which you solve) with 'V = l × w × h' (a general rule true for any box, which you use).
Praise a learner who names the defining feature spontaneously rather than guessing from the look of the symbols.
If a learner reads '3x + 5' only as 'multiply x by 3 and add 5', prompt them to also describe it as a relationship: '5 more than three times a number'.
activities.rationale: Sorting and justifying by a single defining feature sharpens the boundary between easily-confused terms, and reading expressions as relationships rather than instructions follows EEF guidance. An optional interactive sorting tool can highlight or colour the '=' in the last two cards as the learner sorts, making the defining feature visible, but the sorting and verbal justification carry the learning.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase vague responses into language reflecting mathematical structure and encourage pupils to read numerical and algebraic expressions as descriptions of relationships rather than merely instructions to calculate
Proficient students communicate precisely with clear definitions, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and specify units of measure
learnerActions: Sort three cards — '3x + 5', '3x + 5 = 11', 'V = l × w × h' — into three bins labelled expression, equation and formula.

For each card, say out loud what makes it belong there: Does it have an equals sign? If it does, is it a statement of equality that is true only for particular values of an unknown (one you solve), or a general rule relating quantities that holds for any values (a formula, which is a special kind of equation)?

Explain the consequence: an expression can be evaluated (worked out once you know the value of the letter) or simplified, but not solved, while an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 can be solved (find the unknown that makes it true).
Test the boundary with a non-example question such as 'Is 3x + 5 an equation? Why not?' and 'What single change would turn 3x + 5 into an equation?'
activities.intendedInsight: The presence and role of '=' is the defining feature: an expression has none, an equation like 3x + 5 = 11 asserts equality for a particular unknown value (and can be solved), and a formula is a special kind of equation that states a general rule relating quantities for any values. The precise term changes what you are allowed to do with the object.

activities.title: Build the radius–diameter–circumference relationship on a circle
feedback: If a learner says the diameter is centre-to-edge, name that as the radius and have them re-mark the diameter all the way across through the centre.
If a learner calls the circumference the 'edge' or 'side', supply the precise term and tie it to 'the distance all the way around'.
Reinforce when a learner states diameter = 2 × radius and can explain why confusing the two matters.
activities.rationale: Attaching precise terms to features of a manipulated or drawn circle makes the relationship felt rather than memorised. An optional live diagram where dragging the radius auto-draws the diameter at twice its length and traces the circumference makes the 2× relationship dynamic; a drawn or physical circle achieves the same with manual marking.
sourceClaims: Proficient students communicate precisely with clear definitions, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and specify units of measure
learnerActions: On a labelled circle, point to and name the radius, the diameter and the circumference in your own words.
State how the radius and diameter are related and justify it: the diameter goes all the way across through the centre and is exactly twice the radius.
Using a drawn or physical circle, mark a radius, then mark the diameter as two radii end-to-end through the centre, then trace the full distance around for the circumference.

Catch a deliberate error: respond to 'the diameter is the distance from the centre to the edge' by correcting it (that is the radius) and explaining what difference the correction makes to any calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: Radius, diameter and circumference name distinct features that stand in a fixed relationship (diameter = 2 × radius), so the words are not interchangeable; swapping radius and diameter gives a wrong answer. For a length such as the circumference it halves or doubles the answer, and for an area it multiplies or divides the answer by 4.

activities.title: Attach the right unit to volume
feedback: If a learner writes just '60', ask '60 what?' and have them add the unit.
If a learner writes '60 cm²' for a volume, point out that cm² measures area (a surface); filling space needs cm³.
Confirm when a learner both gives the correct cubic unit and can say why space-filling means cubic.
activities.rationale: Grounding 'cubed' in a unit-cube model connects the exponent to physically filling space, and insisting on the unit follows the precision standard. The spatial unit-cube model is the one genuinely three-dimensional strand here.
sourceClaims: Proficient students communicate precisely with clear definitions, state the meaning of the symbols they use, and specify units of measure
learnerActions: Work out the volume of a box (e.g. with a unit-cube model, counting how many 1 cm cubes fill it) and write the answer with its unit.
State why the unit is cm³ and not cm² or a bare number: volume fills space in three dimensions, so it is counted in cubic units.
Contrast a volume (cm³) with an area (cm²) for the same figure, saying what each measures.
activities.intendedInsight: A quantity is incomplete without its unit, and the unit must match the dimension: volume fills space so it is measured in cubic units (cm³), distinct from area's square units (cm²).

activities.title: Expert dialogue: justify the precise term
feedback: When a learner slips (expression called an equation, radius called diameter), the questioner asks them to justify, prompting self-correction rather than supplying the answer.
Rephrase a learner's informal response ('the line across') into the formal register ('the diameter') and ask them to reuse it.
activities.rationale: Dialogue that demands justification surfaces the reasoning behind the vocabulary, which sorting alone may not elicit. Rephrasing informal talk into the formal register follows EEF guidance. This complements, rather than replaces, hands-on sorting and manipulation.
sourceClaims: Teachers should rephrase vague responses into language reflecting mathematical structure and encourage pupils to read numerical and algebraic expressions as descriptions of relationships rather than merely instructions to calculate
learnerActions: Respond to an in-role questioner who insists on the exact term: 'Is that an expression or an equation? What makes it one?'
When you use loose language, restate it in precise mathematical terms when asked.
Defend your classification or your circle-part naming with the defining feature, not just the answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to name the defining reason — the role of the equals sign, centre-to-edge versus all-the-way-across — is what distinguishes precise understanding from loose usage.

constraints: A sort-and-label task can check whether a learner picks the right category or label efficiently, but on its own it does not surface the reasoning that defines the terms; pair it with a task or dialogue that asks 'what makes it one?'.
A static labelled diagram or definition list is a useful reference, but it does not let the learner sort, manipulate or justify, so it cannot by itself build the distinctions.
Recognition-only responses (choosing the right label) do not elicit independent construction of a definition; include tasks where the learner states the defining feature in their own words.

A physical unit-cube model or paper circle has real thickness and can be handled; treat it as an approximation to the idealised mathematical figure (which has exact faces/edges or zero thickness) when discussing area versus volume.

Optional interactive features (auto-drawing the diameter at 2× the radius, highlighting the '=', tracing the circumference) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory; a drawn or physical circle and card sorting work equally well.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit: diameter = 2 × radius, centre-to-circumference radius, circumference as distance around, and volume in cm³ versus area in cm² are all internally consistent and correct as stated in the source. No arithmetic or conceptual errors were found to correct.

The original source asserted that a static image 'cannot' teach and that a quiz 'cannot surface the reasoning'; these have been softened to narrowly scoped limits (reference-only vs. construction-eliciting) rather than universal claims about media.

The source's '60 cm³' volume task does not specify the box dimensions; the rewritten activity frames it generically (count unit cubes) and uses 60 only to illustrate bare-number versus unit, so no unverified arithmetic is asserted.

Residual catalog/product vocabulary ('bench', 'screener') is absent from the final learner-facing guidance; a fresh scan confirms no artefactType labels, fit rankings, 'recommended' or quiz-step terms remain.

probeDeeper: Is 3x + 5 an expression, an equation or a formula? What would make it an equation?
Point to the radius, the diameter and the circumference — how are the radius and diameter related?
Is V = l × w × h an expression, equation or formula? Why?
You wrote the volume as 60 — 60 what? Why cm³ and not cm²?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for '3x + 5 is an EXPRESSION' (it has no equals sign; an equation asserts equality like 3x+5=11, and a formula is a general rule like V=l×w×h) and 'the distance from the centre to the edge is the RADIUS; the diameter goes all the way across through the centre and is twice the radius'; and for why it matters (you can solve an equation but only evaluate an expression; confusing radius and diameter halves or doubles the answer). Surfaced for discussion, not scored.

errorPatterns.pattern: Conflates expression, equation and formula — calls 3x + 5 an equation, or uses the terms interchangeably
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort examples by the presence and role of '=' and read expressions as relationships not instructions; an equation asserts equality, a formula is a general rule. Reteach expressing problems algebraically.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels an expression an equation, or cannot say what distinguishes the three

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses circle parts — says the diameter is centre-to-edge (the radius), or calls the circumference the 'edge/side'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Label a circle: radius = centre to circumference, diameter = across through the centre = 2×radius, circumference = the distance around. Reteach naming parts of a circle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Defines the diameter as the radius, or lacks the term circumference

errorPatterns.pattern: Omits the volume unit or uses the wrong dimension — '60' or '60 cm²' for a volume
errorPatterns.nextMove: Volume fills space, so it is measured in cubic units (cm³); contrast with area's cm². Reteach in place.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a volume with no unit or a square unit

responseLevels.gap: Conflates expression/equation/formula, swaps circle parts, and drops or wrong-dimensions the volume unit.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, distinguishes expression, equation and formula and the circle parts with defining reasons, uses cm³ correctly, and explains why the precise term changes what you can do or compute.
responseLevels.partial: When prompted, gives a distinguishing feature (the equals sign; centre-to-edge) but not reliably, or defines one pair while muddling the other.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child said '3x + 5 is an equation', and 'the diameter is the distance from the centre to the edge of a circle.' Are these right? Fix them, and explain the difference each correction makes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A precise child fixes both and names the defining feature — the equals sign, and centre-to-edge versus all-the-way-across; a loose child accepts them. The slips are invisible to numerical work elsewhere, so only attention to the vocabulary and its meaning separates the children.
